title: Tame inertia normal form by roots of normal crossings parameters
statement:
Let $Y$ be a regular Noetherian scheme [def-weil-regular-scheme, pqf-def-locnoeth], let $D\subset Y$ be a reduced normal crossings divisor (etale locally the zero set of a product of distinct regular parameters), and put $U=Y\setminus D$. Let a finite group $G$ act on a normal Noetherian scheme $Z$, and let $q:Z\to Y$ be a finite surjective quotient [def-weil-finite-integral-morphism] with invariant structure sheaf and orbit geometric fibres. Normal means that all local rings are integrally closed domains [def-weil-pbc-normal-ring]. Assume the action is generically free, $q$ is etale over $U$ [def-weil-etale-morphism], and for every geometric point $\bar w$ of $Z$, lying over $w\in Z$, the stabilizer $\operatorname{Stab}_G(\bar w)$ (the geometric inertia group) has order invertible in $\kappa(w)$. Fix a geometric point $\bar z$ above $\bar y$ [def-weil-geometric-point], and put $H=\operatorname{Stab}_G(\bar z)$. There exist pointed affine etale neighbourhoods $W\to Z$, $T=\operatorname{Spec}A\to Y$, a map $W\to T$ over $q$, an integer $n\geq1$ invertible in $A$, boundary equations $t_1,\ldots,t_r$ with $r\geq0$, a primitive root $\zeta\in A^\times$ with $\zeta^n=1$ and all $1-\zeta^a$ invertible for $0<a<n$, and a subgroup $K\subseteq(\mathbf Z/n\mathbf Z)^r$, such that the $t_i$ form part of a regular system of parameters [def-weil-pbc-regular-system-of-parameters] at the selected point and $U\times_YT=D(t_1\cdots t_r)$. Define
$$B=A[x_1,\ldots,x_r]/(x_i^n-t_i)_i,$$
with $(a_i)\in(\mathbf Z/n\mathbf Z)^r$ acting by $x_i\mapsto\zeta^{a_i}x_i$ and fixing $A$. Then $W\cong\operatorname{Spec}(B^K)$ over $T$. On strict localizations [def-weil-pbc-strict-henselization-limit] at the selected points this isomorphism identifies the actual $H$-action with the action induced by the diagonal root group, with
$$H\cong(\mathbf Z/n\mathbf Z)^r/K.$$
The scheme $Z$ is not assumed regular or excellent, $D$ need not be strict globally, and $|G|$ need not be invertible on $Y$. When $r=0$, the selected strict-local cover is the identity and $H=1$. No log structure or logarithmic regularity conclusion is asserted.

source.place: IX Proposition 2.1(i)--(iii), printed pp.133--134, local parameter-root invariant description, applied after strict localization to the inertia group; VI 2.2--2.3, pp.72--73, diagonal root actions. This is the underlying-scheme Abhyankar normal form used in VIII 5.3.8, p.125.

proof.text: Apply the normal-crossings branch atlas with both boundaries equal to $D$. It supplies a pointed affine etale chart $T_0$ with $D_{T_0}=V(t_1\cdots t_r)$, all selected factors vanishing at the selected point and every vanishing sublist belonging to a regular parameter system. Apply the inertia-slice lemma, refining this prescribed $T_0$. We obtain integral regular $T_1$, normal integral $V$, and the $H$-quotient $V\to T_1$, with $V\to Z$ pointed etale and $n=|H|$ invertible on $T_1$. Pull back the equations from $T_0$. Etale preservation of parameter systems and the parameter criterion make $D_{T_1}$ a strict normal crossings boundary. Only $|H|$, not $|G|$, has been inverted.

source.place: IX 2.1, printed p.133, etale-local parameter reduction; inertia reduction as in VI p.74.

proof.text: Write $T_1=\operatorname{Spec}A_1$, $V=\operatorname{Spec}C_1$ and $L_1=\operatorname{Frac}(C_1)$. The slice supplies a connected finite etale $H$-torsor on the complement of $D_{T_1}$. The finite normal cover $V$ is precisely the normalization of $T_1$ in $L_1$: its elements are integral over $A_1$, and any element of $L_1$ integral over $A_1$ is integral over $C_1$, hence belongs to $C_1$ by integral closedness. Thus the parameter-root quotient theorem applies to this torsor and its finite normalization. It produces a further pointed affine etale $T=\operatorname{Spec}A\to T_1$, a pointed affine etale $W\to V$, the specified root $\zeta$, and $K\leq\Gamma=(\mathbf Z/n\mathbf Z)^r$, with $W\simeq\operatorname{Spec}(B^K)$ over $T$. Require its prescribed-parameter refinement clause, so the equations are the pulled-back $t_i$. Compose $W\to V\to Z$; the etale-composition theorem applies to these two etale maps. All neighbourhood and algebra assertions of the item now hold.

source.place: IX 2.1(ii) and local invariant-ring normal form, pp.133–134.

proof.text: Put $R=\mathcal O^{\mathrm{sh}}_{Y,\bar y}$ and $C=\mathcal O^{\mathrm{sh}}_{Z,\bar z}$. Etale invariance identifies the strict local rings of $T$ and $W$ with $R$ and $C$. The slice gives $R=C^H$, $C$ finite normal local over $R$, and the actual faithful $H$-action on $C$. Strict-henselization regularity makes $R$ regular Noetherian local. The strict-henselization cotangent comparison preserves the parameter positions of the $t_i$. Therefore the root-algebra structure theorem applies to $\widetilde B=R[x_i]/(x_i^n-t_i)$: it is a strictly henselian regular local domain, has the same residue field as $R$, and for $F=\operatorname{Frac}(R)$, $E=\operatorname{Frac}(\widetilde B)$ it identifies $\operatorname{Aut}_F(E)$ with the rotations $\Gamma$.

source.place: IX 2.1 local root algebra, p.133; VI 2.2–2.3, pp.72–73.

proof.text: The monic relations give the basis $x^a$, $0\le a_i<n$, of $B$ by successive polynomial division. A rotation $k\in K$ multiplies this basis vector by $\zeta^{\sum k_ia_i}$. Every nontrivial such scalar differs from $1$ by a unit. Hence an invariant element has zero coefficient at every basis vector with nontrivial $K$-character; the remaining basis vectors freely span $B^K$. This calculation commutes with coefficient extension to $R$, so $(B^K)\otimes_A R=\widetilde B^K=:J$. In particular $J$ is finite free over $R$.

source.place: IX 2.1 displayed root algebra and invariant quotient, p.133.

proof.text: The ring $J\subset\widetilde B$ is a domain. The extension $J\subset\widetilde B$ is integral, since the root algebra is already integral over $R\subset J$. Lying over lifts every maximal ideal of $J$ to a prime of $\widetilde B$, and the integral prime-over-maximal theorem makes that prime maximal, so $J$ is local; its residue field is exactly that of $R$, since it lies between that field and the equal residue field of $\widetilde B$. As a finite local algebra over the henselian ring $R$, $J$ is henselian by the finite-algebra product theorem. Thus $J$ is strictly henselian. For a pointed etale $J$-algebra $S$, the selected residue map lands in $k_J$ since that field is separably closed. Apply the henselian-local-target lifting theorem with base and target both $J$ (the identity algebra is module-finite and formally unramified): the residue map lifts uniquely to $S\to J$. Uniqueness makes these maps compatible. Their colimit map retracts $J\to J^{\mathrm{sh}}$. To check the other composite, apply the same lifting bijection with base and target $J^{\mathrm{sh}}$ to each etale algebra $S\otimes_J J^{\mathrm{sh}}$: the composite and its coprojection have equal residue maps, so are equal. Thus the colimit map is inverse. Consequently $\operatorname{Spec}J=W\times_T\operatorname{Spec}R$ is its own strict localization at the selected point. Its map to $W$ is ind-etale (base change of the strict-local structural map), so strict-local invariance identifies $J$ with $C$. This is the strict-local extension of the isomorphism from Step 2; it identifies actual $H$-actions by transfer, without asserting an action of $H$ on $W$ itself.

source.place: IX 2.1 etale-local normal form, pp.133–134; VI p.74 strict-local quotient.

proof.text: Inside $E$ one has $\operatorname{Frac}(J)=E^K$. Indeed, for $u=a/b\in E^K$ with $a,b\in\widetilde B$ and $b\ne0$, put $d=\prod_{k\in K}k(b)$. Then $d\in J$ is nonzero, and $du=a\prod_{k\ne1}k(b)$ is both in $\widetilde B$ and $K$-fixed, hence in $J$. Conversely every fraction of invariant elements is fixed. The same denominator argument for $C$ and $H$ gives $\operatorname{Frac}(C)^H=\operatorname{Frac}(C^H)=F$. The faithful finite $H$-action on $C$ extends faithfully to its fraction field $L$, so the finite-field-action theorem gives $L/F$ Galois of degree $|H|$. The finite-Galois theorem says $|\operatorname{Aut}_F(L)|=[L:F]=|H|$; thus the injective actual action $H\to\operatorname{Aut}_F(L)$ is an isomorphism.

source.place: IX 2.1 normalization and invariant-field argument, pp.133–134; Stacks 09I3 and 09DW.

proof.text: The group $\Gamma$ is abelian, so $K$ is normal. Apply the normal-fixed-field quotient theorem to $E/F$: restriction gives $\Gamma/K\simeq\operatorname{Aut}_F(E^K)$. Steps 5–6 identify $E^K$ with $\operatorname{Frac}(C)$. Compose this restriction isomorphism with the inverse of the actual $H$-action isomorphism in Step 6 to obtain $\Gamma/K\simeq H$. Every rotation preserves $\widetilde B^K$ because it commutes with $K$. If a rotation class corresponds to $h\in H$, their actions agree on the fraction field by construction; therefore they agree on its subring $C=\widetilde B^K$. This proves the claimed equivariance on strict localizations, including its normalization as the actual action. When $r=0$, $\Gamma=1$ and the root algebra and its invariant ring are $R$; hence $C=R$ and $H=1$.

source.place: VI 2.2–2.3 diagonal root action, pp.72–73; IX 2.1, pp.133–134; Stacks 09DW.
